title: ‘The Burning Giants’ Review: An Arcane, Multi-Pronged Mystery About Ethnic Cleansing in Thailand
description: If it’s a bit too easy to group Thai director Phuttiphong Aroonpheng into a post-Apichatpong Weerasethakul wave of cryptic fablemakers, his latest o
body:
If it’s a bit too easy to group Thai director Phuttiphong Aroonpheng into a post-Apichatpong Weerasethakul wave of cryptic fablemakers, his latest only strengthens this association. His third feature “The Burning Giants” is a woozy dystopian mystery, with fog-strewn forests and liquidy purple skies captured by cinematographer Emo Weemhoff in a menacing ayahuasca haze, and the breadcrumbs of a story about the violent ousting of an indigenous people from their ancestral home, scattered widely enough to ensure you’ll get lost in the woods. 
	

	This kind of disorientation isn’t without potency or pleasure, and for a tale of displacement, it’s a fittingly hazy mood. But Aroonpheng’s worldbuilding is arcane to a fault, with no thanks to a weirdly flat rhythm that dulls the excitement of the film’s many narrative swerves. Competing in Venice’s Orizzonti sidebar, it’s a bit of a letdown considering the promise of “Manta Ray,” Aroonpheng’s waterlogged ghost tale, which won the section when it bowed there in 2018. 


	Still, there’s much to admire in a film that’s so defiantly elliptical, and that doesn’t care to hand-hold the non-Thai viewer through its maze. In any case, knowing a little bit about the true-life episode that inspired its fantastical reimagining will certainly help viewers connect with its cryptic choices. The idea for Aroonpheng’s script originated with news of the 2014 murder of Indigenous rights activist Porlajee “Billy” Rakchongcharoen, a member of the mountain-dwelling Karen ethnic group whose language and people are prominent throughout the film. Rakchongcharoen was the spokesperson for a community of Karen folks living in the mountains of west Thailand when they were forcibly evicted by Thai authorities. Arson was reportedly among the cruel methods of dispersal, though the officers’ crimes were denied and ignored by the State.
	

	In the beginning of “The Burning Giants,” a presumed-infected man named Yak (Awat Ratanapintha) scurries through a purgatorial hillside before being captured and detained by armed mountain police wearing gas masks. There’s a mysterious sickness going around, apparently caused by a toxic fog that invisibly burns the skin of whoever comes into contact with it. The indigenous man has some mild skin discoloration but it’s nothing like what’s happened to one of the cops’ own, whose raw, bubbling blisters are seen in agonizing close-up as he writhes in his cot back at the squad’s eerily vacant outpost. 

	There are intimations of a state-sanctioned ethnic cleansing, especially when the soldiers set the man’s cottage aflame. But right before you think you’ve got a grip on what’s happening, Aroonpheng throws us out of this totalitarian thriller and into the seat of a motorbike romance involving one of the more clueless cops from earlier, Lak (Pakapol Srirongmuang), and his sweetheart Aepoh (Phunthida Phairuangkij).

	That’s the first of several remaining hard pivots that reveal Aepoh — and later, her Karen kinswoman Aeva (Waywiree Ittianunkul) — as uprooted victims of the authorities’ clearings. In restrained, naturalistic vignettes, Aepoh mans a market stand and tentatively succumbs to Lak’s overtures; meanwhile, Aeva works as a nanny for a bougie middle-class family while leaving her own young daughter at a makeshift daycare in her own humble part of town. These snapshots into the afterlives of dislocated women and the wary nature of their assimilation into urban society could use far more room to breathe. But onwards the film goes, winding back up the mountain where Aeva searches for Yak and says goodbye to her now-decimated village through a series of long, mournful takes. 

	And as Aroonpheng spins his narrative into a long, misshapen web, the drama involving Yak vanishes behind a cloud of fog and transforms into the film’s most baffling yet bracing detour. The mystic whine of Christine Ott and Mathieu Gabry’s score carries us into a hidden world of ancient Thai deities living inside the mountain’s caves and tunnels. Bedazzled warriors cast in golden, soft-edged lighting glide around sultrily, until a tusked ogre slips away from his masters and (once more) we descend back to civilization. If the first round of assimilation escaped you, well, now we get it again in a more painful, supernatural register. It’s odd for a film that takes so many ambitious shots to keep making the same points; some fog-clearing, in this case, might have clarified the details.

title: Euro-Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch Program Launches at Iberseries & Platino Industria in Madrid (EXCLUSIVE)
description: The Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid has launched the Euro-Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch Program, which assembles a cross-section of m
body:
The Iberseries & Platino Industria confab in Madrid has launched the Euro-Atlantic Series Co-Pro Pitch Program, which assembles a cross-section of mainly European TV projects that seek to advance their development.

	“This is a different initiative from [Iberseries’] Coproduction & Financing Forum, but it maintains the same essence: connecting projects with key partners and accelerating the financing, production and distribution processes of projects in development,” said its general coordinator Rodrigo Ros.
	

	The one-to-one and one-to-many meetings will take place all throughout Tuesday, Sept. 29, followed the next day by a presentation open to the public at the Cineteca Matadero, from 1:00 to 2:00 p.m.


	Backed by prominent production companies, the first edition has assembled a selection committee made up of seasoned professionals from the European audiovisual industry, including Laura Miñarro, VP of international business and coproduction at Buendía Estudios (Spain); Diego del Pozo, head of fiction at Atresmedia Televisión (Spain); José Fragoso, programming head at RTP1 and RTP Internacional (Portugal) and Georges Huercano, development and co-productions manager at RTL (Belgium).

	“The first edition will bring together projects from Spain, Belgium, France, Portugal, Germany, Sweden, Finland, Canada and Uruguay, along with two invited projects thanks to collaboration agreements established with two of Europe’s leading markets and events specializing in series: Göteborg Film Festival, a key reference point for the Nordic audiovisual industry, and Seriencamp, one of the most relevant industry gatherings in Germany,” he noted.
	

	Nine series projects below cover the gamut of genres: from the festival scandal drama in “Callback” to sports docu series “Heartbeats,” thrillers such as “In Memoriam” and “The Invisible Ink” and variations of comedies from a romcom to a heist comedy as well as historical coming-of-age drama, “King of Hearts.”

	The Iberseries & Platino Industria runs Sept. 29- Oct. 2 in Madrid this year.

	“Callback” (Joana Vilapuig, Mirela Vilapuig, Spain)

	Fiction series from Spain’s Funicular Films (“This Is Not Sweden”) and Barcelona-based Left Tackle Films (“Solo Kim”), revolves around director Fran who, at the premiere of her debut feature at a festival, accuses her lead actor and producer Roman of abuse. Title was selected to participate at the Berlinale Series Match. Written by Joana Vilapuig, Mirela Vilapuig and Diego Vega. Marta Baldó produces.



	

	



	“Heartbeats” (“Latidos,” Cristina Molino, Spain)

	Malvalanda’s docu series follows eight elite female athletes as they navigate pregnancy, motherhood and the demands of professional sport. Produced by María del Puy Alvarado, whose company has earned seven Goya nominations and two Oscar nominations, the project has received development funding from the Community of Madrid. Created by del Puy, Azucena Garanto and Alexa Portillo, the series is planned for 2027/28 production. The creators describe motherhood in elite sport as “a novelty and a feat.”

	“In Memoriam – Season 2” (Félix Tétreault, Marie-Claude Blouin, Canada, Belgium)

	The eight-part thriller drama follows six young engineers whose decade-old hazing ritual resurfaces when a former colleague’s will summons them to Spain, where a series of trials exposes the truth behind a murder. Cineflix Rights is attached as distributor. In development with Crave financing, the project seeks European broadcasters, co-production partners and additional financing. Season 1 was Crave’s #1 launch series and won Best Drama Series at the Berlin TV Series Festival.

	“The Invisible Ink” (“La tinta invisible,” César Díaz, Belgium, Uruguay)

	César Díaz’s bilingual political thriller is backed by Belgian company Need Productions and Uruguay’s Guay Films, with Cimarrón Uruguay in advanced talks to join as a production and financing partner. The series follows an exiled revolutionary forced to return to Uruguay and confront his past. Selected for Series Mania’s Series Makers and ACE Series, the project combines political suspense with family drama. Its producers call it “a rare bridge between two regions.”
	



	

	



	“King of Hearts” (Gilles Coulier, Belgium)

	De Wereldvrede’s historical coming-of-age drama follows King Baudouin’s early years on the throne, amid Belgium’s political crisis, family tensions and Congo’s independence. VRT has joined as a development co-producer, with script funding from VAF. The series spans Brussels, Leopoldville, Rome and Madrid, connecting Belgium’s monarchy with Cold War geopolitics and Catholic influence. Producer Gilles De Schryver describes it as “by nature an international story,” designed as a prestige drama with global appeal.

	“Las Palmas My Love” (“Las Palmas mon amour,” France, Spain)

	The romantic comedy is in development as a French-Spanish co-production between Quad Drama and Secuoya Studios. Iris Bucher produces, with ZDF already committed. The project follows a French pop star on the verge of a breakdown who assumes a new identity in the Canary Islands, where she falls for a widowed chef. Bucher describes it as a “Romeo and Juliet situation,” combining romance, comedy and emotional twists with strong international appeal

	“Listen to My Lips” (Daniela Ruah, Portugal, Brazil)

	Six-part character-driven drama from creator-actress Sofia Mirpuri follows Vera, a 29-year-old actress whose progressive hearing loss forces her to confront a life spent in the shadow of her director boyfriend. Set in contemporary Lisbon, the series combines humor, ambition and disability representation. Mirpuri plays the lead. With pilot and series bible completed, the project is seeking writers’ room financing, international co-production partners and a broadcaster, streamer, sales agent or distributor.

	“Sangria” (Horacio Alcalá, Sweden, Finland, Spain)

	The heist comedy from Strive Stories, Sons of Lumiere and The Aurora Project follows a 51-year-old housekeeper and three discarded workers who take on an AI billionaire after automation costs them their livelihoods. Jaakko Hutchings is attached to star. The project has Creative Europe MEDIA slate support. Director and producer Horacio Alcalá calls it “a heist comedy where the weapons are an apron, a lemon and 30 years of being invisible.”



	

	



	“Summer of Love” (Florian Gottschick, Germany)

	The six-part romantic workplace dramedy is being developed by Germany’s Just Make It Production with Polyphon Film. Set in 1967 Hamburg, it follows three women who turn a shipyard computer into Germany’s first matchmaking agency. A German public broadcaster has expressed interest in joining as a minority partner, with discussions underway. Producer Sabine Tettenborn calls it “a warm, funny workplace dramedy” exploring love, identity and intimate data.

title: ‘Babylon Berlin’ Creatives Reflects on Final Season, 13-Year Journey, Past and Present Germany
description:
It only took five weeks to change everything. 

	Following Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor on Jan. 30, 1933, the fifth and final season of hit Ge
body:
It only took five weeks to change everything. 

	Following Hitler’s appointment as Chancellor on Jan. 30, 1933, the fifth and final season of hit German neo-noir series “Babylon Berlin” blends history and fiction one last time as its characters witness the rise of the Nazi Party and its unhinged violence, until Hitler’s full ascension to power after the infamous elections of March 5.

	A dark conclusion for the 13-year-long creative journey that has been this show, but one that had been envisioned from the start by writer-directors Henk Handlogten, Achim von Borries and Tom Tykwer. Returning for the series’ final season along with leads Volker Bruch and Liv Lisa Fries (“Freud’s Last Season”) to work together on one final investigation, Tykwer and von Borries shared their thoughts and emotions ahead of the German release.
	



	

					From left to right, Achim von Borries, Henk Handgloeten, Tom Tykwer. Credits Beta Film, Joachim Gern
	



	“It’s incredible to realize it took so little time to change the system completely,” underlines von Borries. “When we started developing the series, we thought our story would end on Jan. 30. But as we took a closer look at this period of time, it became clear that the few weeks following were as important to this major shift.”


	Yet ahead of this impending doom, the trio refused to succumb to gloom. “We always wanted to tell the story from the perspective of our protagonists, and not as a doomed thing that we know happens,” adds von Borries. “We strongly believe that there were alternatives also. In every moment of time, there are alternatives.” 
	

	In terms of story-telling, this approach connects somehow to the tragedy of the Titanic, adds Tykwer. “But because we stay so intensely with characters that are fighting for something else to happen, it somehow transforms the entire situation. Which is amazing about, of course, fictionalized historical events. You can enter the zone again from while it was happening with a different whole knowledge, and make visible what it means for people nowadays living in this kind of circumstances.” 

	In fact, Europe’s political landscape has changed completely over the course of the serie’s development. And that shift also informed the writers. “During the making of the show,” continues Tykwer, “it became more and more apparent that these topics were also relevant for the people watching it, because it resonated with their political realities and our feelings of growing insecurity.”

	For all its fictionalization of history, “Babylon Berlin’s” last season does resonate eerily with our times, in a way the creators of the show didn’t even expect. Tykwer adds: “As viewers, people started asking themselves: ‘Where am I? Where were these people? How did they experience it?’ And that also infused our writing over the years. We hope that this touches basic universal subjects, yet we had no idea how the political world would change. And this was constantly on our minds.”



	

					‘Babylon Berlin’ Credits Beta Film, Christine Schroeder
									Christine Schroeder
	



	The duo emphasized how much this five-seasons journey was truly a trio effort, with the power of three different voices in the writing room, equally important and very different. Voices that, after separate shootings, would meet again in the editing room, where the German wurst was made. “This whole show became such a massive collaborative effort. Not something that was designed as strategically perfect, but something built out of our collective instincts and influence on one another. I’m telling you,” jokes Tykwer, “They always say writing is re-writing. But editing is definitely re-editing as well, and we kept moving part of episodes again and again!”

	Yet for all this organic, somewhat unplanned process, there was always a moment where the show would come full circle. “There was no chance of postponing our ending,” recalls von Borries, “and we had this big frame always on the back of our minds, from the end of the First World War to the rise to power of the Nazi Party. What did happen during this journey is that we learned to understand our characters better.” “It’s not just about where the series is going,” adds Tykwer, “It’s about characters that grow throughout 48 hours of narrative, and take us with them along the way.”
	

	In its first four seasons, “Babylon Berlin” sold to more than 140 territories and was watched more than 94 million times on Germany’s ARD online platform alone. Gathering multiple awards across the globe, the show wraps this September. “Honestly, it’s a super emotional moment,” shares von Borries. “For us, its the end of a 13-year process and collaboration. Last week, we had a German screening with the crew, and I have to say I was crying during this whole thing because it was so intense. Hundreds of people have worked on this over the course of 10 years, it’s just incredible. I think it’s the biggest thing I’ve made in my life.”

	“Babylon Berlin” wraps with its fifth and final season on Sept. 10, with all episodes being release on ARD’s Mediathek online platform simultaneously. MhZ Choice, which snatched U.S. exclusive rights for the show in early 2024, will stream the last season in 2027.

title: Football Is Back: Seven Key Storylines for the 2026 NFL Season
description:
Sep 9, 2026 12:14am PT	
	

	
		Football Is Back: Seven Key Storylines for the 2026 NFL Season
	
	
			


			
			
	

									DAVID EU
body:
Sep 9, 2026 12:14am PT	
	

	
		Football Is Back: Seven Key Storylines for the 2026 NFL Season
	
	
			


			
			
	

									DAVID EULITT / 2025 Getty Images / John McDonnell
	

		
	
				

	Are you ready for some football?

	Yes, the 2026 NFL season will kick off on the night of Sept. 9 with a Super Bowl LX rematch, as the defending champion Seattle Seahawks square off against the New England Patriots. Over the past two decades, the NFL has emerged as far and away the most popular sport in the U.S., with over 50% of the American population identifying as fans of the league. If that weren’t enough, in 2025, 83 of the top 100 highest-rated TV programs were NFL games, including 23 of the top 24 overall. The Super Bowl attracted 127.7 million viewers, while the Academy Awards drew 17.9 million, and it wasn’t even a good game.

	In order to not embarrass yourself at the water cooler, here are seven key storylines to pay attention to this NFL season, from elite QBs and major offseason moves to newlyweds Taylor Swift & Travis Kelce and the Donald Trump of it all.


			
			
	Will One of These Elite QBs Finally Get Over the Hump?
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	The NFL has no shortage of elite quarterbacks. And most of them have never been to the Super Bowl. 

	Josh Allen, the Buffalo Bills gunslinger and 2024 league MVP, has come close. What’s stopping him? Patrick Mahomes, of course. Or so we thought. As the starting quarterback, Allen has led his team to the AFC Championship twice, in 2020 and 2024, and both times, Mahomes’ Chiefs have eliminated them (not to mention that 2021 comeback in the AFC Divisional playoffs wherein Mahomes drove the Chiefs 44 yards up the field in 13 seconds to tie it, eventually winning in overtime). Last season marked the first in Allen’s career where he found himself in the playoffs sans Mahomes, but the Bills still faced early elimination at the hands of upstart Bo Nix and the Denver Broncos. The Bills lost four consecutive Super Bowls in the ‘90s and have yet to win the big game. Will this finally be Allen and the Bills’ year? 

	On the opposite coast sits Justin Herbert of the Los Angeles Chargers. Widely regarded as one of the top ten quarterbacks in the league, he has yet to lead his team to a single postseason victory. Sure, it’s a team sport, and the Chargers were dealing with a slew of injured players last year, but chucking four interceptions in their playoff matchup against the Texans left critics left even the most ardent Herbert supporters shaking their heads. We’ll see if Herbert can show up when it matters most. 

	The Cincinnati Bengals’ Joe Burrow not only led his team to the 2022 Super Bowl in his second year in the league but has also proven to be Mahomes’ playoff kryptonite. Since that narrow loss to the Rams, the star QB has been plagued by injury after injury, including a torn ligament in his wrist in 2023 and turf toe in 2025.

	And what about the Ravens’ Lamar Jackson, a two-time MVP, and his 3-5 career playoff record?

	During the offseason, the Bengals made several acquisitions to improve their pitiful defense, including flipping a top-ten pick for god tier DT Dexter Lawrence II; the Chargers hired offensive coordinator Mike McDaniel; the Bills replaced longstanding coach Sean McDermott with offensive coordinator Joe Brady; and the Ravens added stud DE Trey Hendrickson after the Maxx Crosby deal blew up. May the best quarterback win.

		
			
			
	New Faces, New Places
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	In addition to one of the league’s best run-stoppers in “Sexy Dexy” joining the Bengals, providing some much-needed leadership to one of the league’s worst defenses, a number of other big offseason moves will change the course of the NFL this season. Myles Garrett finally decamped from the Cleveland Browns, where playoff dreams go to die, for decidedly sunnier pastures in Los Angeles with the Rams — where he’ll be joined by legendary DT Aaron Donald, who’s come out of retirement to wreak havoc on opposing quarterbacks. Let’s pour one out for all the offensive linemen tasked with stopping these two.

	Two of the league’s most talented quarterbacks, Drake Maye of the Patriots and Josh Allen of the Bills, have thankfully been given legitimate no. 1 receiving options in the form of A.J. Brown (who seemed deeply unhappy in Philly) and DJ Moore. Last season, Maye led his team all the way to the Super Bowl in only his second year in the league with a ragtag group of receivers and perennial problem Stefon Diggs. The addition of one of the NFL’s biggest, strongest wideouts will surely pay dividends. Speaking of Stefon Diggs, his old teammate Allen hasn’t had a proper no. 1 option at receiver since he rather foolishly jumped ship. Moore is a major upgrade and could be the missing piece to get Allen to the Big Game. 

	As for the quarterbacks, a number of players will be under center somewhere else this season — most notably the diminutive Kyler Murray, who jumped from the Arizona Cardinals to the Minnesota Vikings (safe to say the JJ McCarthy-replacing-Sam Darnold experiment has not gone swimmingly), where he’ll be firing the pigskin to one of the best receiving corps in the league, led by Justin Jefferson and Jordan Addison. If he can avoid the concussions, Tua Tagovailoa could put up big numbers at indoor Mercedes-Benz Stadium, while the Packers’ backup Malik Willis will be supplanting Tagovailoa as Dolphins QB. It will also be interesting to see how no. 1 draft pick (and Heisman winner) Fernando Mendoza fares on the Raiders, where he’ll be throwing to arguably the best tight end in Brock Bowers. Oh, and Geno Smith has returned to the team that drafted him, the New York Jets, but the less said about that franchise the better.

		
			
			
	The Trump Effect
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	Last season, Donald Trump became the first sitting president to attend a regular season NFL game since 1978, appearing to a mix of cheers and jeers at a matchup between D.C.’s Washington Commanders and the Detroit Lions in Nov. 2025. And then he earned the distinction of being the first sitting president to go to the Super Bowl, which turned out to be a terrible game (coincidence or not?). My money is on Trump hitting up even more NFL games this season since the man cannot help himself — he is obsessed with crowds and TV ratings, and nothing attracts more eyeballs in America than the NFL. Trump, of course, has a long, messy history with the NFL, from serving as a team owner in the flop rival league USFL in the ‘80s to his thwarted attempt to purchase the Buffalo Bills in 2014,which could have changed the course of history, to trying to set up pal Tom Brady with his daughter Ivanka in his heyday. For Trump, the NFL is personal.

	In addition to the gargantuan distraction Trump poses at games, he is also dividing locker rooms. During the offseason, New York Giants QB Jaxson Dart introduced Trump at a political rally in Upstate New York, prompting his teammate, DE Abdul Carter, to tweet out, “Thought this shit was AI.” The two both released statements saying they’d buried the hatchet, with Carter saying, in part, “Some things are bigger than football, and this is one of those things. Jaxson is one of our leaders. He’s the face of our franchise. He not only represents himself and what he does, but he represents all of us, and that goes for anybody who wears a Giants uniform, but if he chooses to align himself with a man like President Trump, it’s my responsibility, based on what I believe and what I stand on, to not only show my teammates that I’m against that, but to show the world.”

	Trump is one of the more divisive figures in American history and his approval rating just hit record lows, so it remains to be seen how much more turmoil he’ll cause in locker rooms across the league.

		
			
			
	Living Legends
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	Don’t it always seem to go that you don’t know what you’ve got ‘til it’s gone? 

	All eyes are on the Kansas City Chiefs following their substandard 2025 season. Mahomes, a three-time Super Bowl champ, had a particularly rough go of it and, in mid-December, tore his ACL and LCL ligaments in his left knee. Rehab reports have been largely positive, with on-the-ground sources claiming that this has been his best training camp yet. Assuming he stays on track, Mahomes is expected to start against the Bo Nix and the Broncos in Week 1. Adding to the excitement is speculation that this will be tight end/Mr. Taylor Swift Travis Kelce’s last year on the field, and he’ll surely want to go out on a high note. Taylor Swift halftime show, anyone?

	In Pittsburgh, the once-great Aaron Rodgers is preparing for his last hurrah, having already confirmed this will be his final season. He first made a name for himself in Green Bay, where he went from second string to starting QB following Brett Favre’s retirement. He had several MVP seasons with the team (and one Super Bowl win) but has taken a reputation hit after several off-field scandals, including lying about receiving the COVID-19 vaccine and 9/11 conspiracy theories. He joined the New York Jets in 2023, where he suffered an Achilles injury during his first series and went 5-12 his second year. In 2025, he made his final move to the Steelers, where he’ll finish out his 21-year career. Let’s see if the podcaster-in-training generates more on-field headlines than off-field ones.

		
			
			
	Rise of the WAGs
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	Taylor Swift first attended a Kansas City Chiefs game in Sept. 2023. From that point on, viewership among women has spiked during every game she’s attended. In a 2025 cover story, Variety Co-Editor-in-Chief Cynthia Littleton spoke with football analyst Mina Kimes, who noted that women who first began watching football to spot Swift in the stands had, slowly but surely, become knowledgeable about the game itself.

	Before that, the NFL barely catered to its female fanbase despite them comprising nearly half its audience. In the post-Swift/Kelce era, the NFL’s marketing strategy has evolved to accommodate women who have recently become fans. Their universal complaint? The lack of fashion. Once the league realized ill-fitting jerseys and vintage shirts that were three sizes too big would no longer cut it, they turned their focus to womenswear brands. Just this year, they’ve rolled out new collections with Abercrombie & Fitch, Victoria’s Secret and Free People. WAG Kristin Juszczyk tapped into the market too — after her DIY gameday looks went viral they caught the attention of Swift, who commissioned a Chiefs jacket and later wore it to a game. The attention — and financial backing — Juszczyk received was enough to launch her own sportswear brand Off Season, geared toward women searching for stylish gameday treads.

	Influencer content — mostly in the form of WAG presence – is also shaping up to play a major role this season. Last month, after Madison Beer (Justin Herbert), Olivia Ponton (Joe Burrow) and Marissa Ayers (Jaxson Dart) were all spotted at team practices within a week of each other, the internet began questioning the timing, particularly given that all three men have a history of keeping their private lives, well, private. Shortly thereafter, Front Office Sports reported that these moments, all caught on camera, were “at least partially coordinated,” fitting into the league’s “helmets-off” marketing effort toward women.

	Casting a dark shadow over this initiative is the league’s long, ongoing history of domestic violence allegations and arrests. The only real way to appeal to women is to ensure that they’re respected (on and off the field).

		
			
			
	Treatment of Women
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	Let’s not mince words: Deshaun Watson starting at quarterback for an NFL team in 2026 is a black eye for the entire league. Putting aside the fact that this man has started 19 games for the Cleveland Browns since signing a 5-year, $230 million contract with the team in 2022 and went on a bizarre rant against his own fan base after a preseason game two weeks ago, Watson has had 24 civil lawsuits filed against him by massage therapists for charges ranging from sexual harassment to sexual assault, including forcible kissing and forced oral copulation. Watson settled 23 of the 24 lawsuits and only received an 11-game suspension and $5 million fine. Despite the Browns drafting a pair of quarterbacks — Dillon Gabriel and Shadeur Sanders — last year, Watson has been named the opening-day starter and a team captain. They could have just held on to Baker Mayfield and avoided all this mess, but this is the Browns after all. Maybe it’s karma for throwing batteries at John Elway.

	If the Watson mess weren’t enough, just last month the NFL announced it had suspended Falcons star linebacker James Pearce Jr. for the first eight games of the season after he was arrested in February and charged with felony aggravated battery with a deadly weapon and felony aggravated stalking against his ex-girlfriend, WNBA superstar Rickea Jackson. Pearce Jr. avoided jail time by cutting a plea deal that included therapy and a no-contact order, and his suspension compelled former player (and current pundit) Ryan Clark to tweet, “The NFL has a domestic violence problem. Even after strengthening its personal conduct policy in 2014, nearly half of the league’s violent-crime cases involve domestic violence.”

	It’s clear that the NFL still has a long way to go when it comes to addressing its domestic violence problem. And the longer it’s ignored, the worse it’s going to get.

		
			
			
	Gambling
			
										
					Image Credit: Getty Images				
					
				

	Late last year, dozens of people were federally indicted for everything from rigging sports betting to conducting high-stakes poker games with mob ties. Then Portland Trailblazers head coach Chauncey Billups and players Terry Rozier and Malik Beasley were nabbed, along with ex-player Damon Jones. That active players like Rozier and Beasley were manipulating games to to appease bettors cast a dark cloud over the league. A major issue, it seems, is that the menu of available bets is so broad that it invites double-dealing. Why would anyone need to bet on a bench player like Jontay Porter scoring less than a few points in a game? And will the NFL be the next big sports league hit by a betting scandal? These players get paid far less than their NBA counterparts and assume far more physical risk.

	On Aug. 27, the NFL announced official multi-year partnerships with three leading sports betting operators: DraftKings, FanDuel and Fanatics Betting and Gaming. The league also held protracted negotiations with the “prediction markets” Kalshi and Polymarket but could not reach an agreement. 

	ABC News subsequently obtained a letter that the NFL sent Kalshi and Polymarket, stating, “It is deeply concerning that bets within the objectionable categories that we identified months ago have been and continue to be listed as contracts on exchanges,” citing “predictions” that are “easily manipulable by a single person” such as if a kicker misses a field goal or a quarterback starts the game by throwing an incomplete pass. “Continuing to list these objectionable contracts threatens the underlying integrity of our games and creates significant risks for our players, coaches, and officials, as well as for those participating on your exchanges,” read the letter.

title: ‘Spider-Man: Brand New Day,’ ‘The Odyssey’ Continue U.K., Ireland Box Office Battle
description: Sony’s superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” retained its box office crown across the U.K. and Ireland for a sixth consecutive weekend,
body:
Sony’s superhero blockbuster “Spider-Man: Brand New Day” retained its box office crown across the U.K. and Ireland for a sixth consecutive weekend, taking £1.6 million ($2.2 million). 

	The performance propelled the film’s cumulative gross to $130.1 million, elevating it to sixth on the territory’s all-time box office chart. The film now sits within striking distance of “Avatar” and “Spider-Man: No Way Home” to break into the all-time top five.
	

	Universal’s epic “The Odyssey” maintained second place in its eighth weekend of release, adding $2 million. The Christopher Nolan-directed feature elevated its total to $111.9 million.


	“Insidious: Out of the Further,” distributed by Sony, secured third place in its third session, collecting $1 million to lift its cume to $8.7 million. Disney’s animated blockbuster “Toy Story 5” rebounded into fourth place in its 12th frame, generating $565,417 to advance its running total to $78.6 million.

	Warner Bros.’ “The End of Oak Street” followed in fifth position in its fourth week, adding $479,055 to bring its running total to $9.3 million. Universal’s “Minions & Monsters” took sixth place in its 10th frame, grossing $473,318 for a cume of $24.4 million.

	True Brit Entertainment’s “The Death of Robin Hood” debuted in seventh position with $427,272 including previews. Disney’s “The Dog Stars” took eighth place in its sophomore frame, adding $411,911 for a cumulative $2.5 million. Altitude’s l”Coyote vs. Acme” placed ninth in its third session with $391,648 and a running total of $2.2 million. Paramount’s “Paw Patrol: The Dino Movie” rounded out the top 10 in its fifth week, banking $371,863 to push its cume to $8.2 million.
	

	In specialized release, Mubi’s “Teenage Sex and Death at Camp Miasma” collected $83,780 over its third frame, lifting its running total to $1.1 million.

	Looking ahead to the upcoming theatrical frame, the release calendar is headlined by high-profile event cinema, studio sequels, and wide indie dramas. Rollouts began with Dogwoof launching the sports documentary “Lomu.” Mid-week debuts include Disney’s concert documentary “Oasis: Don’t Look Back in Anger” releasing into 300+ locations, alongside Studiocanal’s thriller “Pressure” and Lionsgate U.K.’s survival sequel “Fall 2”.

	Thursday releases include the 4K re-issue of “The Passion of the Christ” and Dreamz Entertainment’s Indian action title “Sardar 2.” 

	Wide commercial debuts on Friday opening across 300+ locations are led by Warner Bros.’ fantasy comedy sequel “Practical Magic 2” and Scott Waugh’s action thriller “Runner,” starring Alan Ritchson and Owen Wilson. 

	Specialized, limited, and international rollouts include Break Out Pictures’ “Everybody Digs Bill Evans” across 25+ sites, Olivier Nakache and Éric Toledano’s “Just an Illusion” across 25+ locations, Central City Media’s “Unidentified Murder” across 25+ screens, Tributary’s documentary “Better Go Mad in the Wild,” Dreamz Entertainment’s “Epic,” Miracle Comms and Goldfinch’s music documentary “Eddie Cochran: Don’t Forget Me,” and Peccadillo’s”Blue Film.” 

	Classic films releasing include the 45th anniversary 4K re-issue of “Raiders of the Lost Ark,” the 30th anniversary return of Danny DeVito’s “Matilda,” and BFI Distribution’s new restoration of Claude Chabrol’s “La Femme infidèle (The Unfaithful Wife).” The weekend wraps on Sunday with Anderson Entertainment and Kaleidoscope rolling out the “Space: 1999” 4K restoration double bill.

title: Stefano Knuchel Premieres Final Chapter in 20-Year Hugo Pratt Trilogy with ‘Hugo in Venice’
description: Stefano Knuchel‘s “Il desiderio di essere inutile – Hugo a Venezia” (“A Longing to Be of No Use – Hugo in Venice”) will premiere out of competition
body:
Stefano Knuchel‘s “Il desiderio di essere inutile – Hugo a Venezia” (“A Longing to Be of No Use – Hugo in Venice”) will premiere out of competition at the Venice Film Festival on Sept. 12, in a special screening jointly presented by La Biennale di Venezia, the International Critics’ Week and the Giornate degli Autori. 

	The film is the third and final installment in Knuchel’s trilogy on Italian cartoonist Hugo Pratt, following “Hugo in Africa” (2009) and “Hugo in Argentina” (2021), with its premiere timed ahead of the centennial of Pratt’s birth in 2027.
	

	Knuchel’s earlier work on Pratt has already been recognized on the Lido. “Hugo in Africa” won the Bisato d’Oro for best director in Venice’s Horizons section in 2009, and “Hugo in Argentina” screened in Venice Days in 2021. “Hugo in Venice” is produced by Fiumi Film in co-production with Swiss public broadcaster RSI.


	The film draws on previously unheard recorded conversations between Pratt and his biographer, Dominique Petitfaux, whose book of interviews with the artist supplies the film’s title. It also features participation from key figures connected to Pratt’s legacy, including Patrizia Zanotti, managing director of Cong SA, the company that has managed the rights to Pratt’s work since 1995, and writer Marco Steiner, who worked alongside Pratt in his final years and has since written several continuations of the Corto Maltese story.



	

	



	Variety spoke with Knuchel ahead of the film’s premiere at the 83rd Venice Film Festival.

	The title comes from Petitfaux’s recorded conversations with Pratt. What meaning is born of the translation, “a longing to be of no use”?
	

	Stefano Knuchel: It was a tricky one. The title is beautiful in Italian and French, but “useless” sounds rude in English. It’s really a philosophical provocation. People today try to affirm their own usefulness, and this goes the other way. Like a tarot card, it reads in two directions. One is about transmission, how you inherit a culture and pass something on. Making a 20-year trilogy about transmission is almost punk, working on a completely different rhythm than everything else right now. The other reading comes from Pratt himself. When Petitfaux asked him about people who dismiss comics as a worthless art form, Pratt said that in the face of these people, he was proud to be useless. For the English title we leaned toward a Yeats-like translation, because Pratt loved English culture, and it felt more like poetry that way.

	With this film, your 20-year trilogy on Pratt comes to a close. How did this trilogy change, and change you, along the way?

	Knuchel: Each film has really been about overcoming something. The first was his childhood in Ethiopia with a fascist father, finding his own ethic inside an unethical situation. The second, Argentina, is about becoming an artist, and accepting that as both an opportunity and a burden. The third is about facing your own mortality, and realizing your legacy already came before you, through everything you inherited. I was genuinely scared of that one. Then reality caught up with me. I lost a lot of people in my own family while making it, and I related much more to the questions Pratt was facing near the end. Working on Pratt for 20 years completely changed my relationship to the world. I’m someone who could stay six months on my couch reading a book, and yet I ended up in a conflict zone in Djibouti, in the president’s helicopter. That’s what a great artist does: gives you another view of the world.

	How did you approach reframing Pratt as a literary figure rather than “just” a cartoonist?

	Knuchel: Pratt basically invented the graphic novel. His first long story, “Una Ballata del Mare Salato,” didn’t sell at first, because comics weren’t supposed to be that long. A young editor sent to find out why went to the shops, saw it shelved next to regular comics, and realized it needed an entirely different format. So they published it in black and white, in a large format, and coined the term “graphic novel” so it would sit under “novels,” not comics. That changed the whole perception of the medium. As a kid, three people went into my brain: Fellini, Buñuel and Pratt, and he was the only one not making cinema, yet he brought cinema’s timing into comics. A character leaves the frame and the camera stays on the empty space. That had never been done in comics before. There’s a tiny drawing from one of his books that I blew up huge for the cinema screen and did a slow pan across. And it looked amazing! For many comics, this doesn’t work. It becomes pop art. That’s the balance in Pratt: his hand and his spirit.
	



	

	



	Can you talk about Venice itself in the film’s visual language? Did you prefer treating it biographically, or leaning into the myth of the city?

	Knuchel: Pratt wasn’t born in Venice and didn’t die there. He moved constantly, but Venice got into his psyche. That’s why I open with his own line: “I’m Venetian, so I trust the water.” The water is the subconscious, what you don’t control. I wanted to show Venice as a mirage rising out of the mud of the lagoon, then sinking back into it, because that’s the whole story: you rise from the water for a while, then go back into it forever. I worked with anthropologists rather than a film crew. It took two years to find the right place to get that feeling. Nothing in the documentary is invented. The ’30s archive footage is real and restored. The lodge we enter is the actual lodge he joined in ’74. The Nazi bunkers at the bottom of the lagoon are real too, things people have simply never seen of Venice. At one point I wanted to shoot in the Pacific, but there wasn’t the budget. Then I realized that before Pratt ever went to the Pacific, he dreamed about it for years, in the lagoon. So instead I mirrored archival footage of him in the Pacific with our own footage of Patrizia walking through lagoon spaces that resemble it. I’m happier with that outcome. You make better films without money, because you have to think twice before you shoot.

	What is the lasting reflection you have after such an extensive project, and what do you hope others take away as well?

	Knuchel: Something very simple: the world is an incredible place, and it’s all about how you look at it. Working on Pratt for 20 years took me to Djibouti, Ethiopia, Kuwait, and a whole club of people around the world who loved him for various reasons. Near the end of the film he says that if you understand the exact composition of an eggshell, you can write an entire story within it. He also loved to quote a Persian poet who said “great poets, they come to the world, say one thing, and they leave.” I think that’s what Pratt was saying too: What’s in front of you is beautiful, just look at it. That’s the lesson I keep learning from his work. I hope the film is uplifting. I just want people to feel better.

title: Studio TF1 Set to Launch Medical Drama ‘Dr. Seylan & Cindy’ at Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre
description: Studio TF1 is launching its medical drama “Dr. Seylan & Cindy” at Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre. Filmed in Drôme in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes reg
body:
Studio TF1 is launching its medical drama “Dr. Seylan & Cindy” at Unifrance Rendez-Vous in Le Havre. Filmed in Drôme in the Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes region of Southeastern France, the series stars Natacha Lindinger (“Hard,” “Coco Chanel & Igor Stravinsky”) and Alice Pol (“Sirènes,” “Tricky Old Dogs”).

	Directed by Cathy Verney (“Hard,” “Vernon Subutex”) and Edouard Deluc (“Pétaouchnok,” “Gauguin: Voyage to Tahiti”), the six-episode series introduces us to Louise Seylan (Natacha Lindinger), a neurosurgeon from Paris who returns to her village after her physician father passes away. At the funeral, she meets the wild and irreverent Cindy (Alice Pol), the longtime nurse who helped her father run the only medical facility in town.
	

	Through a series of unexpected events, Louise begrudgingly decides to take over her father’s medical practice with the help of Cindy and deal with the medical emergencies of the local citizens and the craziness that comes with living in a rural town.


	“From the producers of ‘HIP’ comes a feel-good medical series built around an unlikely duo, the meeting of a female ‘Dr. House’ and Phoebe from ‘Friends,’ whose chemistry is impossible to resist. With one case per episode and the warm backdrop of the French countryside, ‘Dr. Seylan & Cindy’ has all the ingredients of TF1’s next breakout hit: exactly the kind of comforting, entertaining show audiences are looking for right now,” said Camille Dupeuble, EVP International TV and Digital Distribution at Studio TF1.

	“Dr. Seylan & Cindy” was created and written by Camélia Acef & Mathilde Pol. It was produced by Itinéraire Productions (“HIP,” “Soleil Noir”) in co-production with TF1, and its producers are Juliette Lassalle, Anthony Lancret and Pierre Laugier. 
	



	

									Cathy Verney and Edouard Deluc. Courtesy of Studio TF1.
	



	Variety interviewed Cathy Verney and Edouard Deluc before its screening in Le Havre.

	How did the idea for the series come about?

	Cathy Verney: Juliette [Lassalle] came to talk to me about the series while she was still in the middle of writing it. If I remember right, two episodes were written and already very polished. I loved the mix of comedy and medical procedural. I was won over right away by Mathilde and Camélia’s writing, sharp, modern, fresh and daring. There was a lot of work on the medical cases to make the investigations complex and realistic, but there was also an entry point built around a strong, funny, unpleasant character, completely at odds with her return to her roots. A genre mashup, sort of a “Connasse” meets “Dr. House,” and that’s what really drew me in.

	Since we met well before production got underway, the promise of being brought into the writing process was also a deciding factor. Being able to bring directing ideas into the writing itself, and getting a handle on the complex psychological stakes the writers had built in, so they could be properly showcased later, saves a lot of time and usually pays off.

	Edouard Deluc: As director of block 2, I come on board once the writing is finished, or close to it. Reading the scripts, which combined rare depth with a light touch, was a genuine pleasure. The quality of the project, the writing, the way the subject was handled, the importance of the subject, the production, and the idea of working in Cathy’s wake, every sign pointed to yes.

	Could you talk about the casting for the series?

	Verney: I met Natacha on “Hard” 17 years ago. It was my first series and we made it together! She was in every scene, we worked hard and laughed a lot. I’d really been looking forward to the chance to work together again. I thought of her almost immediately, and so did our producers. It was a no-brainer, we brought it up with TF1, they were thrilled. I called Natacha, and that was it.

	For Cindy, we needed an actress who was rock-solid in comedy, with a rhythm that played off Natacha’s, someone who could handle digression without losing the audience. We all really wanted Alice, who has that gift, that flair, and that knack for talking a mile a minute. We met to talk through the character and the script, and we knew right away we wanted to do this together.
	

	Medical dramas seem to have unlimited popularity with audiences. Why do you think that is?

	Deluc: The life-or-death stakes, a mirror of our own fragility, the constant tension.

	Verney: The mystery: a diagnosis plays out like an investigation, you search alongside the doctor, you go down the wrong path, you get it wrong. The emotion: recovery, death, birth, you can’t help but identify with it. The intimacy: a consultation drops you straight into a character’s complexity at moments of real vulnerability.

	What were some of the challenges in shooting the series?

	Deluc: First and foremost, it was a pleasure, even a joy, to direct two wonderful actresses, a terrific supporting cast, and a crew that was completely in sync and fully committed, all in service of a story that’s as sharp as it is necessary.

	Verney: The main challenge was finding the right balance between realism and comedy. I wanted the medical desert to feel credible, for people to really feel what it means to live far from a hospital or a doctor, through our characters who work on farms, sometimes very isolated. That sense of scarcity had to feel real for Louise Seylan’s presence to actually matter, without tipping into a grim realism that would have thrown the show off balance.

	That’s why we shot in the Drôme. It has that rural, remote feel, but without being bleak, it’s a sun-drenched region, with hills and gorgeous landscapes. It matched the show’s balance perfectly.

	The other challenge was the medical procedures. We had doctors and ER physicians from the hospital in Montélimar backing us up, and they helped enormously. They coached the crew and the actresses, who trained hard. I found it fascinating to understand the mechanics of a consultation, how a diagnosis takes shape, the precision of every move. I always dreamed of being a doctor, so this immersion meant something extra to me. The neurosurgery scenes were some of the toughest to shoot, but also some of the most exciting; we had to juggle medical accuracy, dramatic pacing, and the very real constraints of a shoot.

title: Tokyo Market Partners With Frontieres, Adding Genre Slate to Gap-Financing Lineup
description: Tokyo market TIFFCOM has struck its first partnership with Frontières, the genre-focused co-production market run by Canada’s Fantasia International
body:
Tokyo market TIFFCOM has struck its first partnership with Frontières, the genre-focused co-production market run by Canada’s Fantasia International Film Festival, adding a wave of horror and thriller titles to the 24 feature projects selected for the seventh Tokyo Gap-Financing Market (TGFM).

	The selection draws from 24 countries and regions across Asia, Europe, South America and North America. TGFM connects feature projects that have already secured at least 60% of their total budget with industry experts for one-on-one meetings aimed at closing financing gaps. All participating projects must include an Asian element.
	

	“Frontières is thrilled to partner with TGFM at TIFFCOM to present our first showcase in Asia,” said Tania Morissette, deputy director of Frontières. “This partnership is a fantastic opportunity to connect our genre filmmaking communities, open new doors for emerging projects, and build meaningful bridges between our markets.”


	The genre lineup has been enriched by projects from Thailand, Nepal and Brazil, among other territories, including Boo Junfeng‘s “Trinity,” a thriller from the Singaporean director and SEAFIC founder-producer Raymond Phathanavirangoon, and Kevin Rahardjo’s “The Land of Jinn,” based on a Kyrgyz legend, from the Indonesian filmmaker and production banner KawanKawan Media. The Frontières Showcase itself comprises five projects, including a body horror film from Brazilian director Gabriela Amaral Almeida, whose earlier work screened in the Tokyo International Film Festival competition, and “The Saddest Stories on Earth” from Vietnamese director Diep Nguyen Hoang, who returns for a second consecutive year following last year’s participation with “1982,” a Busan International Film Festival selection.
	

	This year’s edition also adds a new collaboration with Imagica Group for TGFM’s first open pitch event, scheduled for the afternoon of Oct. 28. 10 of the 24 projects, including five from the Frontières Showcase, will pitch during the session.

	Animation accounts for five projects this year, including an omnibus horror title from the team behind “The Violinist,” this year’s top prizewinner at the Annecy Animation Film Festival. Also on the animation slate is “Back to Tomioka,” adapted from a French graphic novel addressing the Fukushima nuclear power plant accident; a project from OLM animator-turned-director Moriyama Ayumi, a former key animator on the “Pokémon” TV series; and a work from studio P.I.C.S.

	TIFFCOM’s cooperation with Italy’s Cinecittà enters its third year since launching in 2024, bringing three projects including Italian-Japanese co-productions. Among them is Uchiyama Takuya’s “The Blue Breaks”; the director’s previous film, “Numb,” screened in the Panorama section of this year’s Berlin Film Festival.

	Japan has a hand in producing 12 of the 24 selected projects, eight of them originating locally. Japanese participants include directors Matsumoto Yusaku (“Winny”), Yamamoto Hideo (“After the Fever”) and Sakabe Takafumi.

	TGFM has built a track record of alumni success at major festivals, with past participants including “The Violinist,” which went on to win the Cristal Award at Annecy this year, and “Filipiñana,” which took the World Cinema Special Jury Award at Sundance. TGFM is organized by Japan’s Ministry of Economy, Trade and Industry, the Ministry of Internal Affairs and Communications, and Unijapan.

	TGFM will run Oct. 28-30 as part of TIFFCOM’s 2026 edition, affiliated with the Tokyo International Film Festival.

title: ‘Company’ Stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens on the Film’s Power of Stillness
description: The vital act of storytelling drives Casey Affleck’s “Company.” Knowing those stories and the people in them also passes on lessons learned involvin
body: The vital act of storytelling drives Casey Affleck’s “Company.” Knowing those stories and the people in them also passes on lessons learned involving grief, regret and forgiveness. The film premieres in competition at Venice.“Company” stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens, Ben Mendelsohn, Scoot McNairy, Emily Alyn Lind, Caylee Cowan and Atticus Affleck. The film jumps between 1975, 1953 and 1903, connected by stories in each era. Much of the film involves just two actors in a shot, or one actor in a beautifully composed shot.“When Casey sets up the camera, you know by the angles that he’s shooting from that it’s going to be much more intimate,” says Nolte.Nolte’s Tom is an old man living alone. It’s winter, and he sees a young woman passed out on the snow outside his isolated cabin. He brings Alice (Cowan) in, warms her up and she tells him a story about a couple living in a cabin quite like his in 1903.“It was the script, and it was so delicate,” Nolte says of what drew him to the project. “It had these silences and gaps, and the storytelling was obvious. I just found that intriguing. It wasn’t like any script that normally comes in. You know, it was one of those special ones.”Nolte didn’t want to play Tom as necessarily a hermit, though, as we do discover his story as the film unspools. “I looked at him as somebody that wanted to not be with humanity in general. He was a reclusive, and he lived in isolation, and he’d probably be a trapper.”Affleck’s direction is quite intentional, with each scene meticulously framed and lit, allowing stillness to permeate. Nolte’s expressive eyes and face do a lot of the work in each scene as Alice talks. “It was really about listening, just really listening to the story,” he says.In the 1903 segment, Clemens and McNairy play a couple on an isolated farm, who, like Tom, find and rescue a young person from the snow. Caleb (Atticus Affleck) intrigues Rebecca (Clemens), as he brags about his world travels and personal philosophy with a familiar mix of confidence and insecurity — she’s wary, and his presence creates delicious tension.“As I’ve gotten older, and I’ve worked more in the industry, I’ve started to learn the power of a two shot, and I’ve also started to learn that you need really skilled professionals to execute that in a powerful way,” she says. “You need an incredible cinematographer who we have on this film, Marcell Rév — everything was so beautiful.”Clemens says that working with Casey is “what you dream of” because he is an Oscar-winning actor himself.“Directors will often do a two shot, but then they’ll cover it as well. But if you have two actors who are in an environment where they’re supported, then you can have a really powerful scene, and you can see our whole bodies,” Clemens says of the framing, noting that she and her colleagues had to use their whole bodies. “We tell this whole story from the shins up. It wouldn’t be executed in the way it was if we didn’t have Casey trusting us.”Clemens brought a “Buddha-like” demeanor and maternal depth and empathy to Rebecca, whereas Atticus Affleck had to leave everyone wondering about his truth. Clemens says that while he was well-prepared for the film, and “rehearsed intensely,” his performance was natural and “didn’t feel like a performance … He was amazing.”Have some people in Hollywood figured out how to continue to spotlight Hollywood’s greats? “I’m 86, and real limited in the kind of roles I can play now, but I find that without the work, there just isn’t any reason to keep on going,” says Nolte, who has more projects on deck. “You know your creativity is tied into it, and as long as I’m physically capable, I encourage them to consider me. I haven’t thought about retiring.”

schema.headline: ‘Company’ Stars Nick Nolte, Adelaide Clemens on the Film’s Power of Stillness

title: ‘A Common Story’ Review: A Stunningly Played Study of a Couple Whose Inability to Articulate Their Emotions Drives Them Apart
description: Far too often, relationship dramas devolve into screaming matches with a predictable crescendo that exhausts both actors and audiences: They’re usin
body:
Far too often, relationship dramas devolve into screaming matches with a predictable crescendo that exhausts both actors and audiences: They’re using words, but since few writers have the caustic wit of Edward Albee, what they say is more tiresome than trenchant. Perhaps because debuting director Anna Foglietta is first an actor, she understands that silences are more powerful than screeches, even more so when a couple want to express themselves but just can’t find the words. “A Common Story” is a revelation, not just in an Italian film landscape that too often falls back on verbal assaults, but more broadly, thanks to Foglietta’s sensitivity to the spaces between speech, and the superlative performances from Alba Rohrwacher and Guido Caprino, who have never been better.
	

	This sensitivity to voids is revealed in the opening montage, consisting of empty rooms in university buildings, their vacant stillness a troubling indication of absence. It’s the perfect visualization of the empty-nest syndrome experienced by parents Erika (Rohrwacher) and Mauro (Caprino), bringing their only child Irene (Ksenia Borzak) to college. She’s probably the first member of the family to seek higher education, and mom and dad are super proud. Once back home, they fall into their usual patterns: Mauro works in construction with his father Marcello (Elio De Capitani), and Erika is a supermarket cashier.


	Her days always had a structure that reflected her sense of purpose: she’d get up early each morning to bake a bundt cake for breakfast, check in on her mother Altea (Caterina Casini) after work to bring groceries, clean the house, cook the meals. She was useful, and being useful signified she had a role to fill that brought meaning to her life. Now she’s nearly 45, her daughter is out of the house, and she finds herself suddenly adrift without the self-analytical tools to understand what she’s feeling.
	

	Being needed is her reason for waking up in the morning, but Irene is away and self-sufficient Altea is busy with her friends. Perhaps if she could talk about her feelings with Mauro, they’d be able to negotiate the changes together, but notwithstanding a deep love, they’re not people who’ve ever talked about their personal psychology. Unequipped to find the words that could identify her state of mind, Erika begins to fall apart.

	The building blocks of “A Common Story” can be found in countless feminist texts describing the lack of self-worth felt by women whose circumscribed lives seem meaningless when their perceived usefulness is over. But what about the women unable to articulate those emotions, who don’t have access to such texts and for whom the words “mental health provider” might as well be gibberish? Erika is incapable of understanding her depression because she can’t name it, and without the vocabulary she’s unable to share her despair with Mauro, who watches his wife’s disintegration with bewilderment.

	As a man, he’s meant to hold everything together; after all, he’s in construction, he fixes things. But he can’t fix this. Making matters worse, his father’s constant barbs have emasculated him, and when he learns that Marcello sold the business without letting him know, it feels like his role as the anchor of the family has been smashed. Following a humiliation at a family luncheon, Erika and Mauro have an argument; Foglietta first discreetly shoots them at a distance, through the windows of their parked car, then as Erika starts to shout, the angle shifts to the other side, until the camera is very close and the meltdown is as raw as it’s going to get.

	It’s a wrenching moment, and a rare one in a film with barely any cuts within a scene (DP Andrea Benjamin Manenti’s careful framing meaningfully creates barriers within the fixed field of vision). It’s also the only time their voices are raised, yet they still can’t find words to convey their vulnerability. Filling the quivering void is their intense need for each other, and an inability to understand how to make themselves whole again.

	Home alone, no longer driven to bake a cake or organize the house, Erika calls a telemarketer after seeing an infomercial for a face cream. The slick saleswoman asks questions about her skin type, which she can’t answer because she’s never thought about herself that way before, and after excitedly imagining what this product will do, she hangs up disillusioned: no longer able to fulfill the roles of daughter and mother, she also can’t become the kind of woman shaped by a consumer-driven society. 
	

	The scene highlights Rohrwacher’s delicate vulnerability and her masterful way of capturing Erika’s inner life, at once hollowed out yet in turmoil. It’s the character’s perplexity that’s so heartrending, perfectly matched by Caprino’s subtlety in conveying Mauro’s incomprehension at what’s happening to his marriage. With eyes, body language and the charged spaces between words, the two performers show us a couple on the verge of collapse, whose love for one another holds out the promise of salvation.

schema.headline: ‘A Common Story’ Review: A Stunningly Played Study of a Couple Whose Inability to Articulate Their Emotions Drives Them Apart

title: NBA Star Tyler Herro's Ex Slams Him As She Sues For Custody, Support
description:
NBA Star Tyler Herro
                          Ex Katya Slams Him As She Seeks Child Custody, $$$
body:
NBA Star Tyler Herro
                          Ex Katya Slams Him As She Seeks Child Custody, $$$
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            NBA star Tyler Herro and his baby mama Katya Henry have split, and it's already getting nasty ... the exes are duking it out in court over custody and support after their bitter breakup, TMZ has learned.
      
    
            TMZ obtained dueling lawsuits filed by Tyler and Katya. The exes share two minor kids ... a daughter born in 2021 and a son born in 2023 ... so this is no simple split.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            In his filing, Tyler asked the court to set up a parenting schedule and determine how much he should pay in child support. The Milwaukee Bucks star said he had been voluntarily paying his ex support since she gave birth.
      
    
            Tyler dismissed his case days later.
      

            Katya filed her own petition claiming she had been in a romantic relationship with Tyler for nearly 7 years. She claimed she had been the primary caregiver and made most of the decisions for the kids.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            In her filing, Katya asked the court for primary custody. She said she wanted their kids to see Tyler, but due to his "historical conduct," which she "intentionally omitted" out of respect for him, "safeguards and parameters should be implemented on a temporary and permanent basis in order to ensure the safety and well-being" of the kids.
      
    
            Katya said there is a large disparity in income due to Tyler being a professional athlete, who earns a substantial sum of money.
      
    
            The case is ongoing.

title: Sophie Rain: Man Who Broke Into Her Florida Home Goes MIA After 'Blood Oath' Claim
description:
OnlyFans Model Sophie Rain
                          Man Who Allegedly Broke Into Her House Goes MIA .
body:
OnlyFans Model Sophie Rain
                          Man Who Allegedly Broke Into Her House Goes MIA ...
                          After He Told Officials They Took a Blood Oath
                      
                  
                                                                        Published 
                              September 9, 2026
                            1:00 AM PDT
                                                                            
              
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Sophie Rain's alleged burglar made some concerning statements about the OnlyFans model at a crisis center … only months after cops say he tried to break into her home ... TMZ has learned.
      
    
            According to court docs, obtained by TMZ, the man, Connor Litka, made the remarks to a staff member at the crisis center. The docs say Connor said that in July 2025 he stopped taking his psychiatric medication.
      
    
      
        
              
    
    
            A staff member at the crisis center says he reported to an employee that he and his girlfriend Sophie took a "blood oath" and it was an "intense experience." The report said Connor told staff he wanted to get out of "here" and claimed he wanted to leave South Bend, Indiana, and go back to "Florida to be with Sophie."
      

            The docs say Connor believed he was no longer on probation and that he was still sending Sophie money, at least $500.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            The report also said Connor's mother has been calling the center because she is concerned about his increasingly erratic behavior and is unsure how to help him. The crisis center staffer said they remained concerned he would continue to escalate his behavior due to his history and current manic symptoms.
      
    
            Per the court docs, Connor was recently arrested for domestic battery against a woman and failed a drug test.
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            As TMZ first reported, Connor was arrested in February 2025 after law enforcement says he attempted to break into Sophie and her friend's Florida rental home. Sources say Sophie returned home from attending Super Bowl parties to find her windows smashed and Connor inside the home.
      
    
            The SWAT team launched into action and got the man out of the home. He was later sentenced to 5 years' probation
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                  
      
    
            Sophie tells TMZ ... "This situation has been deeply frightening for me and my family. I have never taken a 'blood oath' with this individual, and any belief that we have a personal relationship is completely untrue."
      
    
            She adds ... "I sincerely hope he receives the treatment and support he needs, but my priority has to be protecting my safety and the people around me. Because this is an ongoing legal and security matter, I cannot discuss specific precautions being taken."

schema.headline: Sophie Rain: Man Who Broke Into Her Florida Home Goes MIA After 'Blood Oath' Claim

title: Jim Geoghan, 'Suite Life of Zack & Cody' Co-Creator, Dead at 79
description:
'Suite Life of Zack & Cody'
                          Co-Creator Jim Geoghan Dead at 79
body:
'Suite Life of Zack & Cody'
                          Co-Creator Jim Geoghan Dead at 79
                      
      
    
                  
          
                          
                
                                  
      
    
            Jim Geoghan, co-creator and executive producer of the Disney Channel sitcom "The Suite Life of Zack & Cody," has died.
      
    
            His daughter, Genevieve Geoghan, confirmed to TMZ that the executive producer passed away on Sunday in Los Angeles. He was battling dementia.
      
    
            'Suite Life' was a beloved kids' show responsible for launching the careers of Ashley Tisdale, Brenda Song, plus Dylan and Cole Sprouse.
      

            The series earned Jim a pair of Emmy nominations in 2007 and '08 for Outstanding Children's Program.
      
    
            Jim's other credits include writing for shows like "The Facts of Life," "Silver Spoons," and "The Van Dyke Show" ... just to name a few.
      
    
            He also wrote a couple plays ... "Only Kidding" ran off Broadway for 500 performances, and "Light Sensitive" has run for over 40 performances across the country after starting in San Diego.
      
    
            Jim is survived by his wife and daughter.
      
    
            He was 79.
      
    
            RIP
